This is a minor quibble, but words are sometimes important and - who knows - maybe somebody finding themselves in trouble would be more informed by knowing the difference.

Caveat: I am not a legalfag, so this could have minor to major errors - please correct as needed.

Bail:
Bail is a means of ensuring that the defendant/suspect will return to court to face the charges. The more risky the person is of skipping out on trial, or the more brutal the crime, the more likely that bail will be set higher. Higher profile cases also typically get large bails, along with rich people that wouldn't be too damaged by a small bail - ie, someone with $100million having a bail of $1mill isn't a big deal.

Bail is set as a "promise" to appear in court. Bail is collateral and is returned once the precedings are over - win or lose. Bail is the "get out of jail" promise for the length of the trial.

Some states/courts allow portions of bail to be paid, others demand the whole thing. For example, one state could set a bail of 100k, but only need 15k to get out of jail - along with collateral for the rest. If the defendant doesn't appear at trial, the state keeps the 15k and then also gets the rest of the collateral.

Kyle's case is a full bail case - meaning Kyle had to put up $2million cash to get out of jail. All the donations (hopefully to legit sites) went toward that.

Bail is set at a pre-trial hearing pretty close to arrest. After bail is set, it can be paid at any time.

Pay bail: get out of jail

Don't/can't pay bail: don't get out of jail

Bonds:

Some states recognize that most people do not have tons of cash on hand to pay high bails. Keeping people in jail just because they cannot afford the bail can be considered cruel.

These states then allow bondsmen to step in and pay the bail. A bondsman will post all of the necessary bail for a certain percent up front, between 10-20% or whatever (YMMV).

The bondsmen work just like bail, except the defendant pays the bondsman and the bondsman posts the bail. The bondsman keeps the fee after the trial is over.

For example, if bail is set at 1million in a bond state, the defendant/family/etc would then raise 100k and pay that to the bondsman - never to see that money again - and the bondsman would then post the 1million to the court. If the defendant skips court, the bondsman then loses the 1mill - but will hire bounty hunters to track down the defendant and get their money back.

Kyle was held without bond in Illinois on the charges there, but then extradited to WI to face those charges. WI is a no bond state, which is why the 2million cash bail was needed.

When the trial ends, with whatever outcome, Kyle gets that 2million back.

If you donated to any "bail" fund for Kyle, then you need to recognize that it was probably a scam, because Kyle (or lawyers or family) will keep the money and probably not be able to track everyone down for refunds.
